title: Case report: ALK inhibitor-induced transformation of ALK fusion-positive lung adenocarcinoma to large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma
author: Rui Zhong; Xinyue Wang; Jinhua Xu; Shuai Wang; Ying Liu; Hui Li
text:
Abstract
The transformation of lung adenocarcinoma into large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) in terms of genotype and histology has been described as a mechanism of acquired resistance to epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI). However, this phenomenon is exceedingly rare in anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive lung adenocarcinoma. Here, we report a case of an ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma patient who developed resistance following sequential treatment with the ALK-TKI alectinib and lorlatinib, accompanied by histological transformation to LCNEC and concurrent genetic alterations including TP53 deletion, CDKN2A deletion, and MYC amplification. This case expands the spectrum of ALK-TKI resistance mechanisms and highlights the potential value of exploring combinatorial approaches incorporating immunotherapy, antiangiogenic therapy, and chemotherapy for the management of such cases.
Subject terms: Cancer, Oncology
Introduction
ALK-echinoderm microtubule-associated protein-like 4 (EML4) fusion occurs in approximately 5% of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases1. While ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) showed superior efficacy over conventional chemotherapy2,3, and significantly extended median progression-free survival (mPFS) to over 30 months4, nonetheless, acquired resistance remains an inevitable clinical challenge. The primary resistance mechanisms in ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma include diverse secondary ALK mutations, such as G1202R5, bypass signaling activation (such as EGFR, MET, c-KIT, SRC, RAS/MAPK, and SHP2 mutations)6, MET amplification7, and histologic transformation to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) or squamous cell carcinoma6. Nevertheless, studies of ALK-TKI resistance in ALK-positive patients with respect to transformation from lung adenocarcinoma to LCNEC remain extremely rare, as evidenced by recent case series and reports8,9. Here, we present a case of ALK fusion-positive lung adenocarcinoma that underwent histological and genotypic transformation to LCNEC following sequential treatment with the ALK-TKIs alectinib and lorlatinib, and discuss potential resistance mechanisms and subsequent therapeutic strategies.
Case Reports
An adult patient admitted to Jilin Cancer Hospital with a chief complaint of persistent cough and left-sided limb weakness. Whole-body PET/CT performed on August, 2023, revealed a 6.5 × 4.5 cm mass adjacent to the left lower lobe hilum, accompanied by metastases in the left lower lobe, hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes (stations 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8), bone (T10 vertebra and right ilium), and brain (right frontal lobe, 2.0 cm × 2.4 cm; parietal lobe, maximum diameter 1.1 cm) (Fig. 1A). Bronchoscopic biopsy pathology confirmed lung adenocarcinoma (stage cT4N2M1c IVB), and immunohistochemical staining (IHC) showed CK (+), Ki-67 (30% + ), TTF-1 (+), NapsinA (+), P40 (-), CK5/6 (-), and CD8 (+) (Fig. 1B). On September, 2023, next-generation sequencing (NGS) with a 1021-gene panel (GenePlus, Beijing, China) identified an EML4::ALK fusion (2.4%) and EPCAM gene point mutation along with other genomic alterations of uncertain significance (detailed in Table 1) The tumor mutational burden (TMB) was low (0.75 muts/Mb), with microsatellite stable (MSS) status (Table 1) The patient initiated temozolomide for brain metastasis control combined with alectinib on September, 2023. After one month of combination therapy, treatment was transitioned to alectinib monotherapy. Approximately three months into the treatment, follow-up examinations revealed significant tumor regression: the left lung lesion decreased to 2.1×1.1 cm, the right frontal lobe metastasis reduced to 1.0 cm, and the right parietal lobe metastasis shrank to subcentimeter size (<5 mm). The bone metastases as well as the left hilar and mediastinal lymph node metastases remained stable (Fig. 1C) On January, 2024, brain MRI revealed progression of the right parietal lobe metastasis (approximately 1.5 cm in diameter), while other lesions remained stable (Fig. 1D). Therefore, the PFS was only five months. The patient underwent cranial stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) and continued alectinib therapy. Over the subsequent two months, gradual enlargement was observed in the primary left lung lesion (3.4 × 2.9 cm) and left lower lobe metastasis (Fig. 1E). Consequently, alectinib was discontinued in March 2024 and replaced with lorlatinib. A follow-up scan on July, 2024, demonstrated further enlargement of the left lung lesion (4.8 × 4.0 cm) and slight progression of the right parietal lobe metastasis (0.9 cm) (Fig. 1F). Repeated bronchoscopic biopsy pathological examinations revealed IHC features as follows: vimentin (+), CK5/6 (-), P40 (-), TTF-1 (+), NapsinA (-), CD56 (-), synaptophysin (-), Ki-67 (90% + ), CK ( + ), CK7 (-), CK20 (-), Villin (-), INSM1 (partially +), and PD-L1 (50%+) (Fig. 2A). Combined with morphological characteristics—the tumor cells exhibit a nested growth pattern with organoid structures, the tumor cells are large with abundant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli—the findings lead to the diagnosis of LCNEC. NGS (1021 panel) confirmed the persistence of the EML4::ALK fusion (35% variant allele frequency) and revealed acquired genomic alterations including TP53 mutation, and copy number gains in MYC and losses in CDKN2A and MTAP, which have been implicated in neuroendocrine differentiation and tumor progression. Other alterations are listed in Table 1. The TMB remained low (7.5 muts/Mb) with MSS status. The presence of wild-type RB1 is more consistent with the NSCLC-like subtype of LCNEC10,11. The patient was then switched from lorlatinib monotherapy to another regimen regarding to toripalimab combined with etoposide and carboplatin. After two cycles, the response was assessed as stable disease (SD). By the fourth cycle, the patient developed thoracic vertebral metastasis-related pain, with slight enlargement of the primary left lung lesion and progression of the right parietal metastasis (1.5 cm), classified as progressive disease (PD) (Fig. 2B). A revised one-cycle regimen of bevacizumab, toripalimab, and nab-paclitaxel was delivered alongside thoracic spine radiotherapy. Symptomatic relief was achieved, and follow-up imaging demonstrated partial response (PR): reduction of the primary left lung lesion to 2.3 × 1.5 cm and the right parietal metastasis to 1.1 cm, with stability at other sites (Fig. 2C). The patient maintained PR after two additional cycles of this regimen and remains under ongoing therapy (Fig. 2D). Fig. 2E showed the patient’s treatment history.

Discussion
Histologic transformation to high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas, primarily SCLC, represents the most common form of TKI-induced lineage plasticity in NSCLC, with SCLC transformation predominantly observed in EGFR-mutant NSCLC6. Morphologically, transformed SCLC typically exhibits classic neuroendocrine features, accompanied by positive immunohistochemical staining for neuroendocrine markers, such as synaptophysin and chromogranin12. Molecular profiling of these transformed tumors frequently revealed concurrent TP53 and RB1 mutations13–15. Two primary hypotheses have been proposed to explain this phenomenon. The clonal selection theory posited that NSCLC and SCLC components may coexist at tumor initiation, with TKI pressure favoring the outgrowth of SCLC clones6,16. Alternatively, the transdifferentiation theory suggested that nearly all EGFR-mutated adenocarcinomas that transform into SCLC retain their original EGFR activating mutations, implying plasticity of common progenitor cells, alveolar type II cells, capable of divergent differentiation17. Notably, histologic transformation from lung adenocarcinoma to LCNEC represented a rarer resistance mechanism compared to SCLC conversion18–21. LCNEC transformation may be driven by genetic alterations, particularly TP53 and RB1 inactivation22. Similar to SCLC transformation, a subclonal cell population harboring molecular biomarkers of neuroendocrine differentiation present at the baseline and not detectable upon conventional histological examination, underwent progressive clonal evolution under the selective pressure of EGFR-TKI treatment, ultimately leading to a pathological transition towards high-grade LCNEC23.
Emerging evidence suggested that histologic transformation, a recognized resistance mechanism in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma treated with EGFR-TKI, may also occur in ALK-positive tumors following ALK-TKI24,25. A growing number of case reports indeed underscore that neuroendocrine lineage transformation, though rare, is a tangible resistance mechanism in ALK-rearranged NSCLC. The most documented pattern is transformation to SCLC. For instance, studies have documented SCLC transformation in ALK-positive patients after developing resistance to alectinib, accompanied by elevated serum levels of ProGRP and NSE26. The observation of SCLC transformation during alectinib treatment, rather than crizotinib therapy, might be attributed to alectinib’s higher selectivity and potent tumor-suppressive effects compared to crizotinib, potentially favoring the outgrowth of pre-existing neuroendocrine subclones under therapeutic pressure4. Beyond SCLC, transformation to or de novo presentation of ALK-positive LCNEC is increasingly recognized. The clinical behavior of these tumors is heterogeneous. Notably, some cases demonstrate retained ALK pathway dependency, showing significant clinical responses to ALK-TKIs, such as alectinib, lorlatinib, and brigatinib27–29. However, recent evidence highlights a more complex and aggressive resistance phenotype. A pivotal study in 2024 reported that a rare dual resistance mechanism wherein ALK-rearranged NSCLC transformed into high-grade LCNEC after ALK-TKI treatment in three cases, concurrently acquiring on-target ALK kinase domain mutations8.
Our present case aligns with and extends this understanding. Integrated NGS and IHC analysis revealed that the transformed LCNEC tumor retained the original EML4::ALK fusion, co-occurring with an acquired TP53 deletion and upregulated expression of INSM1, a key neuroendocrine transcription factor. This genomic and phenotypic profile suggested partial transformation of adenocarcinoma to LCNEC under therapeutic pressure, potentially driven by clonal evolution favoring neuroendocrine differentiation. This hypothesis aligns with the pathological observation of limited tumor cellularity in post-progression biopsies, which may have hindered detection of residual adenocarcinoma components, reflecting sampling limitations in heterogeneous tumors. Notably, our patient acquired additional genomic alterations post-transformation, including CDKN2A deletion, MTAP deletion, and MYC gain, among others. Gardner and colleagues found that the barrier to histological transformation converges on tolerance to MYC, which was implicated as a lineage-specific driver of the pulmonary neuroendocrine cell30. Epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) may represent another potential mechanism of lineage plasticity in ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma following targeted therapy resistance, as evidenced by studies31–33.This hypothesis is supported by the positive expression of the mesenchymal marker vimentin in PD samples in our results. Furthermore, the disappearance of the EPCAM indel variant in PD samples samples indicates altered cellular plasticity. Collectively, these molecular changes highlight the multifaceted nature of resistance mechanisms in ALK-positive tumors.
This case involved a patient initially diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma through small biopsy, with subsequent NGS revealing an ALK fusion mutation. First-line alectinib treatment achieved PR, but progression-free survival (PFS) was only 5 months, significantly shorter than the median PFS of 41.6 months reported in the ALESIA trial for alectinib-treated patients34. Furthermore, disease progression occurred just 4 months after switching to lorlatinib, suggesting possible pre-existing adenocarcinoma-LCNEC heterogeneity at initial diagnosis. Current clinical management of LCNEC typically follows SCLC-like chemotherapy regimens. While immune checkpoint inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in SCLC, their role in LCNEC remains investigational (NCT05470595, NCT05470595). Notably, PD-L1 testing in this patient showed 50% expression, indicating potential immunotherapy benefit. Bevacizumab, a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody targeting VEGF, may improve disease control rates and overall response in patients with brain metastases compared to conventional therapies35,36. Based on these considerations, the patient received four cycles of LCNEC-standard etoposide/carboplatin chemotherapy combined with toripalimab and bevacizumab, achieving SD. Subsequent thoracic spine radiotherapy was administered for worsening bone pain. Given potential continued benefit from anti-angiogenic/immunotherapy, treatment was maintained with toripalimab, bevacizumab plus nab-paclitaxel (a broad-spectrum antineoplastic agent), resulting in marked tumor regression (PR) after just one cycle. In conclusion, this case brought insights that combined immunotherapy, anti-angiogenic therapy, and chemotherapy may have potential efficacy in ALK-positive NSCLC patients with LCNEC transformation, however, it merits further investigation in prospective cohorts to confirm their generalizability. Despite these insights, it is important to consider that the limitations of this study primarily lie in the idiosyncratic patient factors inherent to a single case. Furthermore, our mechanistic insights remain descriptive and lack of in-depth mechanistic exploration to define the direct role of the identified molecular changes in driving neuroendocrine transformation and mediating drug resistance. In the future, the identified molecular events (e.g., EML4::ALK fusion, TP53 mutation, wild-type RB1) require functional validation to establish their direct role in driving neuroendocrine transformation and resistance.
In summary, this case suggested that histological transformation from ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma to LCNEC may represent a mechanism of TKI resistance. In the era of multi-targeted therapy, repeat biopsies of progressing lesions should be considered to detect potential histological shifts. Additionally, baseline NGS molecular profiling was critical to identify concomitant mutations, as these may predict a higher risk of transformation and resistance. A comprehensive therapeutic strategy, tailored to such findings, could optimize first-line PFS, improve survival in ALK fusion-positive patients, and guide more precise treatment approaches.
Methods
Ethics approval
The study was approved by Institutional Review Board (IRB) for the Jilin Cancer Hospital, the IRB number was 202506-004-01. The patient gave informed consent for the analysis and publication of the data.
Histopathology and IHC
Hematoxylin and eosin staining was performed on 5 μm sections generated from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue. All pathology slides were reviewed by a pathologist with expertise in lung cancer pathology. Immunohistochemical primary antibodies against Ki67 (ZM-0166), CK5/6(ZM-0313), NapsinA (ZM-0337), TTF-1 (ZM-0262), P40 (ZM-0472), vimentin (ZM0260), CD8 (ZA-0508), CK (ZM-0069), CD56 (ZM-0057), synaptophysin (ZM-0246), CK7 (ZM-0071), CK20 (ZM-0148), Villin (ZM-0261), and INSM1 (ZA-0695) were purchased from ZSGB-Bio (Beijing, China). PD-L1 staining using E1L3N antibody (AmoyDx, 8.17.0002, China). A performed in Bench Mark ULTRA fully automated IHC (Ventana).
Next-generation sequencing (NGS)
DNA was extracted from FFPE samples using Maxwell® RSC DNA FFPE Kit (Promega, Madison, WI, USA) with quality control for quantity and fragment size. 1 μg each of genomic DNA extracted from FFPE specimen was sheared to 300-bp fragments with a Covaris S2 ultrasonicator (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA), purified with beads, and quantified. A volume of 20–80 ng DNA from plasma were used for library construction. Indexed Illumina NGS libraries were prepared from tumor DNA using the KAPA Library Preparation Kit (Kapa Biosystems, Wilmington, MA, USA). A panel of 1021 cancer-related genes which were previously described37,38. Sequencing was carried out using Gene+ Seq-2000.
